core: The Enlightenment as an 18th-century (rooted in the 17th) intellectual movement privileging reason, science, and human progress over tradition and superstition
Core ideas: natural rights, the social contract and government by consent, separation of powers, religious tolerance and free speech, empiricism building on the Scientific Revolution

Key thinkers and what each is known for: Locke (natural rights, consent), Montesquieu (separation of powers), Rousseau (social contract, general will/popular sovereignty), Voltaire (tolerance, free speech), Wollstonecraft (women's rights)
The movement's limits and contradictions stated honestly: exclusion of women, and figures who proclaimed universal rights while rationalizing racism and slavery
Its influence on the coming political revolutions (named, not owned)
supporting: Kant's 'What Is Enlightenment?' (1784) and the motto sapere aude ('dare to know')
Newton's Principia (1687) as a catalyst linking the Scientific Revolution to Enlightenment method
outOfScope: The political revolutions themselves (American, French) — handed off to history:foundations:revolutions / :american-revolution
The US Constitution as a document — history:foundations:constitution

claims.claim: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement of the eighteenth century (with seventeenth-century roots) that emphasized reason, empirical science, and human progress over inherited tradition, superstition, and unquestioned authority.

The Enlightenment took its method and confidence from the Scientific Revolution of the 16th-17th centuries; Newton's Principia (1687) modeled how observation and mathematics could yield universal laws.

John Locke (1632-1704), in Two Treatises of Government (published 1689, dated 1690), argued that people hold natural rights to life, liberty, and property and that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed.
Montesquieu (1689-1755), in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), argued for separating a state's legislative, executive, and judicial powers to protect liberty and check the government.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-1778), in The Social Contract (1762), argued that a state is legitimate only when guided by the 'general will' of the people as a whole rather than an elite minority — a principle of popular sovereignty.
Voltaire (1694-1778) is known for defending religious toleration and freedom of speech, in works including his Treatise on Tolerance and the 1759 satire Candide.

Mary Wollstonecraft (1759-1797), in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), argued that women only appeared less rational because they were denied education, and that they should be educated as reasoning beings and equals.

The Enlightenment's universalist rhetoric coexisted with deep contradictions: most women were excluded from it (Rousseau held women were subordinate and belonged in the domestic sphere), and some figures used social-contract reasoning to defend slavery, while racism developed alongside proclamations of universal rights.

Immanuel Kant (1724-1804), in 'What Is Enlightenment?' (1784), defined enlightenment as humanity's emergence from self-incurred immaturity, capturing the motto sapere aude ('dare to know / think for yourself').
Enlightenment ideas of natural rights, consent, and popular sovereignty helped inspire the political revolutions of the later 18th century.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Publication date of Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689 vs 1690).
positions: OpenStax cites 1690 (the date printed on the title page)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The work appeared anonymously late in 1689 but carried 1690 on its title page. The lesson states 'published 1689, dated 1690' to be accurate to both.

positions: Locke condemned slavery in the Two Treatises
Locke invested in the Royal African Company and helped draft the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, which entrenched slaveholding power
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats Enlightenment contradiction at the level of the movement (universal-rights rhetoric alongside rationalizations of slavery and exclusion of women) rather than adjudicating Locke's personal record, which scholars still debate.

Supports the movement's core ideas, the thinkers and their signature contributions (Locke life/liberty/property and consent; Montesquieu separation of powers and Spirit of the Laws 1748; Rousseau general will; Voltaire tolerance/free speech and Candide 1759), and the explicit statement that most women were excluded and that some used social-contract theory to defend slavery. Facts synthesized; prose written originally.

sourceRecords.title: The Enlightenment (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed reference. Supports the period (18th century, roughly ending with the French Revolution), the origin in the Scientific Revolution (Newton's Principia 1687), core themes (reason, empiricism, natural rights/consent, separation of powers, religious tolerance), and Kant's definition of enlightenment and sapere aude. Reference only; no wording reproduced.
